concepts.title: अहम् — I

explanations.kidFriendly: In Sanskrit, 'I' is अहम् — pronounced aham. This word belongs to the Pronouns group, so you'll meet it again when you study other words in the same family. Try saying it out loud: aham.
explanations.textbook: अहम् (aham). First person singular pronoun, nominative case. In Hindi this corresponds to मैं; in English, 'I'.
explanations.expert: First person singular pronoun, nominative case. Words in the Pronouns category share patterns of declension or usage — comparing अहम् with other entries in the same category will reveal the underlying paradigm. The transliteration aham uses IAST conventions: long vowels are marked with a macron (ā, ī, ū), and retroflex sounds with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ, ṣ).

concepts.reasoning: In Sanskrit, 'I' is rendered as अहम् (aham). First person singular pronoun, nominative case.

useCases.description: When someone says 'aham' in a Sanskrit conversation, they mean 'I'.

chapters.title: वन्दे भारतमातरम् — Vande Bharatamataram (I Salute the Motherland)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 1. Two children ask their mother the meaning of the song 'Vande Mataram'; she explains its meaning, its author Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, and the verses that praise Bharat as a loving mother — crowned by the Himalaya, her feet washed by the ocean, green with crops watered by farmers' sweat.

topics.title: वन्दे मातरम् — The Song and Its Story
topics.summary: What 'Vande Mataram' means, who wrote it, and the novel it comes from.

concepts.title: वन्दे मातरम् — I bow to the Mother

explanations.oneLine: वन्दे मातरम् (vande mātaram) — 'I bow to the Mother' / 'I praise the Motherland'.
explanations.kidFriendly: वन्दे मातरम् means 'I bow to the Mother'. In this chapter the 'Mother' is भारतमाता — Mother India. वन्दे comes from the root meaning 'to greet / to praise', and मातरम् is the accusative of मातृ (mother).
explanations.textbook: वन्दे मातरम् — 'I salute/praise the Mother'. वन्दे = 'I greet/praise' (from वन्द्); मातरम् = mother (accusative singular of मातृ). The chapter explains the line as 'अहं मातुः वन्दनं करोमि' — 'I offer salutation to the Mother'.
explanations.expert: वन्दे is the first-person singular present of the root वन्द् ('to praise, salute'). मातरम् is the accusative singular of the feminine ṛ-stem मातृ; the accusative marks the Mother as the object of veneration. IAST: vande mātaram, with the long ā shown by a macron.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter opens with two children asking their mother what the song 'वन्दे मातरम्' means; she explains it as offering salutation to the Motherland.

useCases.title: Grammar bridge

concepts.title: बङ्किमचन्द्रः चट्टोपाध्यायः — Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay

explanations.oneLine: The poet बङ्किमचन्द्रः चट्टोपाध्यायः wrote 'वन्दे मातरम्'.
explanations.kidFriendly: The song was written by the great patriot बङ्किमचन्द्रः चट्टोपाध्यायः (Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay). The chapter tells us he placed it in a novel he wrote in the year 1882.
explanations.textbook: महान् देशभक्तः बङ्किमचन्द्रः चट्टोपाध्यायः — 'the great patriot Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay'. The chapter states he wrote the novel 'आनन्दमठः' (Anandamath) in 1882 (१८८२ तमे वर्षे), and the song वन्दे मातरम् appears within it.
explanations.expert: देशभक्तः = 'patriot' (देश 'country' + भक्तः 'devotee'). The chapter dates the novel आनन्दमठः to १८८२ — note Sanskrit/Devanagari numerals: १८८२ = 1882.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's dialogue directly names Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay as the author and 1882 as the year of his novel आनन्दमठः, in which the song appears.

concepts.beyondTheBook: आनन्दमठः (Anandamath) is a famous Bangla novel; the song वन्दे मातरम् is written in Sanskrit within a largely Bangla work — the chapter notes the song uses both languages (संस्कृतं बाङ्ग्ला च).

concepts.title: उपन्यासः — Novel

explanations.kidFriendly: उपन्यासम् means a 'novel' — a long book that tells a story. The chapter glossary explains it as बृहत्कथारूपम् ('in the form of a big story'). The song वन्दे मातरम् appears inside such a novel.
explanations.textbook: उपन्यासम् — accusative of उपन्यासः, 'novel'. Glossed in the chapter as बृहत्कथारूपम् ('a large narrative work'). Hindi: उपन्यास.
explanations.expert: उपन्यासः literally suggests 'a placing-near / narration'; in modern usage it means the literary form 'novel'. The accusative उपन्यासम् is used because the author 'wrote (a) novel' — the novel is the object of लिखितवान्.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary lists उपन्यासम् with the meaning 'Novel' (Hindi: उपन्यास को), used when saying Bankim Chandra wrote a novel.

concepts.title: जिज्ञासा — Curiosity

explanations.kidFriendly: जिज्ञासा means curiosity — the wish to know something. In the chapter, the children feel जिज्ञासा about who wrote the song. The glossary explains it as ज्ञातुम् इच्छा ('the wish to know').
explanations.textbook: जिज्ञासा — 'desire to know, curiosity'. Glossed in the chapter as ज्ञातुम् इच्छा. It is a feminine noun; Hindi: जानने की इच्छा.
explanations.expert: जिज्ञासा is a desiderative formation from the root ज्ञा ('to know') — the desiderative stem जिज्ञास- expresses 'wishing to know', a classic Sanskrit grammatical pattern.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary gives जिज्ञासा = 'Curiosity' (ज्ञातुम् इच्छा), describing the children's wish to learn about the song.

useCases.title: Name your feeling
useCases.description: When you really want to find something out, that feeling is जिज्ञासा.

useCases.title: Root spotting
useCases.description: जिज्ञासा comes from ज्ञा 'to know' — the same root as ज्ञानम् 'knowledge'.

useCases.title: In the chapter
useCases.description: The children's जिज्ञासा drives the whole opening dialogue.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The desiderative (wishing-to-do) is a productive Sanskrit pattern: from पा 'drink' comes पिपासा 'thirst (wish to drink)', just as ज्ञा gives जिज्ञासा.

solutionSteps: The chapter explains वन्दे मातरम् as 'अहं मातुः वन्दनं करोमि' — 'I offer salutation to the Mother'.
वन्दे = 'I praise/greet'; मातरम् = 'Mother' (here, the Motherland).
commonMistakes: Don't confuse वन्दे ('I praise') with words for singing or seeing — वन्द् specifically means to salute or praise.

solutionSteps: The chapter names the great patriot बङ्किमचन्द्रः चट्टोपाध्यायः as the author.
He placed the song inside his novel आनन्दमठः.
commonMistakes: Kālidāsa and Pāṇini are famous Sanskrit figures but are not the author of this song.

questions.prompt: In which year did Bankim Chandra write the novel आनन्दमठः?
solutionSteps: The chapter states '१८८२ तमे वर्षे' — in the year 1882.
१८८२ in Devanagari numerals is 1882.
commonMistakes: 1857 and 1947 are other famous years in Indian history, but the chapter specifically says 1882.

solutionSteps: The chapter glossary gives जिज्ञासा = ज्ञातुम् इच्छा, 'the wish to know'.
It comes from the root ज्ञा, 'to know'.
commonMistakes: जिज्ञासा is specifically the desire to KNOW — not a general feeling like anger or tiredness.

topics.title: भारतमातुः वर्णनम् — Words for the Motherland
topics.summary: Key vocabulary from the poem describing Bharat: mountains, ocean, holy places, crops, and farmers.

concepts.title: पर्वतराजः — The King of Mountains

explanations.kidFriendly: पर्वतराजः means 'the king of mountains'. It is made of पर्वत ('mountain') + राजः ('king'). In the poem it describes the mighty Himālaya standing over Bharat.
explanations.textbook: पर्वतराजः — 'king of mountains', glossed in the chapter as पर्वतानां राजा. It refers to the Himālaya, pictured as a crown (मुकुटरूपेण) upon the Motherland.
explanations.expert: पर्वतराजः is a tatpuruṣa compound: पर्वतानां राजा ('king OF mountains'), the genitive relation folded into a compound. The poem uses मुकुटरूपेण ('as a crown') for how the Himālaya sits atop Bharat.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary gives पर्वतराजः = पर्वतानां राजा; in the poem the Himālaya is the crown of the Motherland.

useCases.title: Picture the image
useCases.description: The Himālaya sits on Bharat's head like a मुकुट (crown) — that is the पर्वतराजः.

useCases.title: Break the compound
useCases.description: पर्वत (mountain) + राजः (king) = 'king of mountains'.

useCases.title: Answer an exercise
useCases.description: The chapter exercise asks 'पर्वतराजः कः?' — the king of mountains is the Himālaya.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Compounds like पर्वतराजः ('king of mountains') and नदीराजः are common in Sanskrit poetry to praise the greatest of a kind.

concepts.title: रत्नाकरः — The Ocean

explanations.kidFriendly: रत्नाकरः means the ocean. It literally means 'the mine of jewels' (रत्न 'jewel' + आकरः 'mine'), because the sea holds many treasures. The chapter glossary gives its meaning simply as समुद्रः ('sea').
explanations.textbook: रत्नाकरः — 'ocean', glossed in the chapter as समुद्रः. Literally रत्न ('jewel') + आकरः ('mine/source') — 'the source of jewels'.
explanations.expert: रत्नाकरः is a bahuvrīhi/tatpuruṣa-style compound naming the sea by a quality (jewel-bearing). The poem says the ocean washes the Mother's feet (चरणौ प्रक्षालयति).

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary gives रत्नाकरः = समुद्रः ('sea'); the poem pictures the ocean washing Bharatamātā's feet.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet रत्नाकरः in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam), Chapter 1 — its glossary gives the meaning 'Sea/Ocean'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see रत्नाकरः, recall it means 'Sea/Ocean'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try framing a simple Sanskrit sentence using रत्नाकरः ('Sea/Ocean').

concepts.beyondTheBook: The ocean is called रत्नाकर because, in Indian tradition, the churning of the sea (समुद्रमन्थन) produced many jewels and treasures.

concepts.title: तीर्थक्षेत्राणि — Holy Places

explanations.kidFriendly: तीर्थक्षेत्राणि means holy places — the sacred pilgrimage sites of Bharat. The chapter glossary explains it as पुण्यक्षेत्राणि ('places of merit').
explanations.textbook: तीर्थक्षेत्राणि — neuter plural, 'holy/pilgrimage places', glossed as पुण्यक्षेत्राणि. People come from many regions (विविधेभ्यः प्रदेशेभ्यः) to these places.
explanations.expert: तीर्थक्षेत्राणि is तीर्थ ('sacred crossing/pilgrimage') + क्षेत्र ('field/place'), neuter plural. तीर्थ originally means a 'ford' — a place to cross a river — and came to mean a sacred crossing-point.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary gives तीर्थक्षेत्राणि = पुण्यक्षेत्राणि ('holy places'); the lesson lists many ancient pilgrimage sites and their modern names.

useCases.title: Map old and new names
useCases.description: The chapter pairs ancient names with modern ones — e.g. काशी = वाराणसी.

useCases.title: Understand the build
useCases.description: तीर्थ (sacred crossing) + क्षेत्र (place) = 'holy place'.

useCases.title: Answer an exercise
useCases.description: An exercise asks why people come from many regions — to visit these तीर्थक्षेत्राणि.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The chapter includes a fascinating table of प्राचीन (ancient) versus आधुनिक (modern) place-names — e.g. इन्द्रप्रस्थम् = देहली, पाटलीपुत्रम् = पटना.

concepts.title: सस्यश्यामला — Green With Crops

explanations.kidFriendly: सस्यश्यामला describes Bharat as deep-green with crops and plants. It is सस्य ('crops') + श्यामला ('dark/green'). The chapter glosses it as सस्यैः घनश्यामा — 'darkened (green) by crops'.
explanations.textbook: सस्यश्यामला — 'densely covered with green crops', glossed as सस्यैः घनश्यामा. A feminine adjective describing भारतमाता / भारतभूमिः.
explanations.expert: सस्यश्यामला is सस्य ('grain, crops') + श्यामला ('dusky-green'); श्यामला feminine pairs with the feminine भूमिः/माता. The word evokes fertile, crop-rich land.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary gives सस्यश्यामला = सस्यैः घनश्यामा ('densely green with crops'), describing the fertile Motherland.

useCases.title: Picture fertile fields
useCases.description: सस्यश्यामला paints Bharat as lush and green with crops.

useCases.title: Split the compound
useCases.description: सस्य (crops) + श्यामला (dark-green) = 'green with crops'.

useCases.title: Link to farmers
useCases.description: The land is green because farmers (कृषकबान्धवाः) water it with their sweat.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The word echoes the famous national-song line; श्यामल ('dusky') is also a name of beauty in Sanskrit, so सस्यश्यामला is 'beautiful-dark with crops'.

concepts.title: स्वेदबिन्दुभिः सिञ्चन्ति — Watered by Sweat-Drops

explanations.oneLine: स्वेदबिन्दुभिः सिञ्चन्ति — '(farmers) sprinkle/water (the land) with drops of sweat'.
explanations.kidFriendly: This phrase praises farmers: कृषकबान्धवाः ('our farmer brothers') water the Motherland स्वेदबिन्दुभिः ('with drops of sweat'). सिञ्चन्ति means 'they sprinkle/irrigate'.
explanations.textbook: स्वेदबिन्दुभिः ('with sweat-drops', instrumental plural) सिञ्चन्ति ('they water/sprinkle'). The chapter glosses सिञ्चन्ति as सिञ्चनं कुर्वन्ति and स्वेदबिन्दुभिः as घर्मस्य जलकणैः.
explanations.expert: स्वेदबिन्दुभिः is the instrumental plural of स्वेदबिन्दु (स्वेद 'sweat' + बिन्दु 'drop') — 'by means of sweat-drops'. सिञ्चन्ति is 3rd-person plural present of सिच् ('to sprinkle, irrigate'). The instrumental marks the means.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter glossary glosses सिञ्चन्ति = सिञ्चनं कुर्वन्ति ('they irrigate') and स्वेदबिन्दुभिः = घर्मस्य जलकणैः ('with drops of sweat'); together they honour farmers' labour.

useCases.title: Honour farmers
useCases.description: The line teaches gratitude — farmers literally water the land with their sweat.

useCases.title: Spot the instrumental
useCases.description: स्वेदबिन्दुभिः ('with sweat-drops') is instrumental — it answers 'by what means?'.

useCases.title: Answer an exercise
useCases.description: An exercise asks 'कृषकबान्धवाः भारतभूमिं कैः सिञ्चन्ति?' — with their sweat-drops.

concepts.beyondTheBook: सिच् ('to sprinkle') is the same root behind अभिषेक ('consecration by sprinkling') — the everyday act of watering and the sacred act of anointing share a root.

questions.prompt: 'पर्वतराजः' (the king of mountains) refers to which mountain?
solutionSteps: पर्वतराजः = पर्वतानां राजा, 'king of mountains'.
The poem pictures it as the crown (मुकुट) of Bharat — the Himālaya.
commonMistakes: The Vindhya, Aravalli and Sahyadri are real ranges, but the 'king of mountains / crown of Bharat' is the Himālaya.

solutionSteps: The chapter glossary gives रत्नाकरः = समुद्रः.
Literally 'mine of jewels' — a poetic name for the sea.
commonMistakes: रत्नाकरः is not a river (नदी) — it is the great sea that washes the Mother's feet.

solutionSteps: The chapter glossary gives तीर्थक्षेत्राणि = पुण्यक्षेत्राणि ('places of merit').
People travel from many regions to visit them.
commonMistakes: तीर्थ means a sacred crossing — these are holy places, not ordinary fields or markets.

solutionSteps: The chapter glossary gives सस्यश्यामला = सस्यैः घनश्यामा ('densely green with crops').
सस्य = crops, श्यामला = dark-green.
commonMistakes: The word specifically means green WITH CROPS — not snow-covered or barren.

questions.prompt: With what do the farmers (कृषकबान्धवाः) water the Motherland?
solutionSteps: The chapter says farmers सिञ्चन्ति ('water') the land स्वेदबिन्दुभिः ('with sweat-drops').
The glossary glosses स्वेदबिन्दुभिः = घर्मस्य जलकणैः ('with drops of sweat').
commonMistakes: The poem's point is the farmers' own labour — their sweat — not ordinary water.

chapters.title: नित्यं पिबामः सुभाषितरसम् — Nityam Pibamah Subhashitarasam (Let Us Daily Drink the Nectar of Wise Sayings)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 2. A garland of subhashitas (wise sayings): the five 'va' qualities that earn respect, the six faults to give up, how body/mind/soul/intellect are each purified, and how a pot — and knowledge — fills drop by drop. Plus key vocabulary on inspiration, procrastination, enmity and good company.

topics.title: सुभाषितानि — Wise Sayings
topics.summary: The famous moral verses of the chapter and what each teaches.

concepts.title: सुभाषितम् — A Wise Saying

explanations.oneLine: सुभाषितम् (subhāṣitam) — a 'well-spoken' verse: a short saying full of wisdom.
explanations.kidFriendly: A सुभाषितम् is a 'well-said' thing — su ('good') + bhāṣita ('spoken'). These are short Sanskrit verses that pack a life-lesson into a few lines. The chapter's title says we should 'daily drink the nectar (रसम्) of subhashitas'.
explanations.textbook: सुभाषितम् — 'a well-spoken (saying)', सु + भाषित. The chapter frames them as सुवचनानि ('good sayings') composed by wise people (श्रेष्ठजनैः) for the growth of human values (मानवानां विविधमूल्यानां विकासाय).
explanations.expert: सुभाषितम् is a past-participle compound: सु ('well') + भाषित ('spoken', from भाष्). The chapter's title नित्यं पिबामः सुभाषितरसम् means 'daily let us drink the nectar of subhashitas' — रसम् ('essence/nectar') as the object.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter explains सुभाषितानि as good sayings (सुवचनानि) spoken by the wise to help develop human values.

useCases.title: Collect sayings
useCases.description: Start a notebook of subhashitas you like — that is exactly what this chapter encourages.

useCases.title: Break the word
useCases.description: सु ('good') + भाषित ('spoken') = 'well-said'.

useCases.title: Daily habit
useCases.description: The title urges drinking the 'nectar' of a wise saying every day.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The subhashita tradition is huge — collections like the Subhāṣita-ratna-bhāṇḍāgāra gather thousands of these gem-like verses.

concepts.title: पञ्च वकाराः — The Five 'Va' Qualities

explanations.oneLine: A person is honoured by five qualities beginning with 'व': विद्या, वपुस्, वाणी, वस्त्र, विनय.
explanations.kidFriendly: One verse says a person becomes respected (पूजितः) by five things that start with the sound 'व' (va): विद्यया (knowledge), वपुषा (body/health), वाचा (speech), वस्त्रेण (dress), and विनयेन (humility/good manners).
explanations.textbook: वकारैः पञ्चभिर्युक्तो नरो भवति पूजितः — 'joined with the five va-s, a person becomes honoured': विद्यया, वपुषा, वाचा, वस्त्रेण, विनयेन च.
explanations.expert: वकारैः = 'by the (sounds) va' (instrumental plural of वकार, 'the letter व'). The verse is a mnemonic: all five virtues conveniently begin with व, making them easy to remember.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's exercise asks 'नरः कतिभिः वकारैः पूजितः भवति?' — a person is honoured by FIVE 'va' qualities.

useCases.title: Self-check list
useCases.description: Knowledge, health, speech, dress, humility — score yourself gently on the five va-s.

useCases.title: Memory trick
useCases.description: All five start with व — that is why the verse is easy to recall.

useCases.title: Answer the exercise
useCases.description: कतिभिः वकारैः? → पञ्चभिः (five).

concepts.beyondTheBook: Sound-based mnemonics (all words starting with one letter) are a favourite device of Sanskrit subhashitas — they make moral lists stick.

concepts.title: षड् दोषाः — The Six Faults to Give Up

explanations.oneLine: One who wants prosperity must give up six faults: sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, laziness, procrastination.
explanations.kidFriendly: Another verse lists षड् दोषाः ('six faults') a person who desires success (भूतिम् इच्छता) should discard (हातव्याः): निद्रा (over-sleep), तन्द्रा (drowsiness), भयम् (fear), क्रोधः (anger), आलस्यम् (laziness), दीर्घसूत्रता (putting things off).
explanations.textbook: षड् दोषाः पुरुषेणेह हातव्या भूतिमिच्छता — निद्रा तन्द्रा भयं क्रोधः आलस्यं दीर्घसूत्रता. Six faults to be abandoned by one wishing prosperity.
explanations.expert: हातव्याः is a gerundive (kṛtya) of हा ('to abandon') — 'to-be-given-up'; भूतिम् इच्छता is 'by one desiring prosperity' (present participle, instrumental). The verse pairs a duty (give up faults) with its reward (भूति).

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's exercise asks 'पुरुषेण कति दोषाः हातव्याः?' — SIX faults are to be given up by a person who wants to prosper.

useCases.title: Habit audit
useCases.description: Check yourself against the six: too much sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, laziness, delay.

useCases.title: Grammar note
useCases.description: हातव्याः = 'to-be-abandoned' — a gerundive expressing obligation.

useCases.title: Answer the exercise
useCases.description: कति दोषाः हातव्याः? → षड् (six).

concepts.beyondTheBook: Compare these six faults with the modern idea of 'procrastination' (दीर्घसूत्रता) — Sanskrit named the habit of endlessly delaying work over a thousand years ago.

concepts.title: शुद्धि — How Different Things Are Purified

explanations.oneLine: Body is cleaned by water, the mind by truth, the soul by learning and austerity, the intellect by knowledge.
explanations.kidFriendly: A famous verse explains that different parts of us are 'cleaned' in different ways: अद्भिः (by water) the body (गात्राणि); सत्येन (by truth) the mind (मनः); विद्यातपोभ्यां (by learning and austerity) the soul (भूतात्मा); and ज्ञानेन (by knowledge) the intellect (बुद्धिः).
explanations.textbook: अद्भिर्गात्राणि शुध्यन्ति मनः सत्येन शुध्यति, विद्यातपोभ्यां भूतात्मा बुद्धिर्ज्ञानेन शुध्यति — body by water, mind by truth, soul by learning+austerity, intellect by knowledge.
explanations.expert: Each line uses the instrumental case for the means of purification: अद्भिः ('by waters', irregular instrumental plural of अप्), सत्येन, विद्यातपोभ्यां (dual — 'by learning and austerity'), ज्ञानेन. शुध्यति is from शुध् ('to become pure').

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's exercise asks 'बुद्धिः केन शुध्यति?' — the intellect is purified by ज्ञानेन (knowledge).

useCases.title: Four kinds of clean
useCases.description: Water cleans the body; truth cleans the mind — a memorable life-lesson.

useCases.title: Spot the instrumental
useCases.description: अद्भिः, सत्येन, ज्ञानेन all answer 'by what means?'.

useCases.title: Answer the exercise
useCases.description: बुद्धिः केन शुध्यति? → ज्ञानेन.

concepts.beyondTheBook: अद्भिः is a classic irregular form — the word अप् ('water') is used only in the plural and has unusual case endings worth learning.

concepts.title: जलबिन्दुनिपातेन — Drop by Drop the Pot Fills

explanations.oneLine: जलबिन्दुनिपातेन क्रमशः पूर्यते घटः — 'drop by falling drop, the pot gradually fills'.
explanations.kidFriendly: A beautiful verse teaches patience: जलबिन्दुनिपातेन ('by the falling of water-drops') क्रमशः ('step by step') पूर्यते ('is filled') घटः ('the pot'). Small efforts, repeated, add up to a great result — and the verse applies the same to knowledge, dharma, and wealth.
explanations.textbook: जलबिन्दुनिपातेन क्रमशः पूर्यते घटः — by drop-by-drop falling the pot fills gradually; the verse extends this to the slow accumulation of vidyā, dharma and dhana.
explanations.expert: निपातेन ('by falling', instrumental of निपात) and पूर्यते (passive, 'is filled', from पॄ) make the means→result structure. The image of the घट (pot) filling drop by drop is one of the most-quoted in Indian pedagogy.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's exercise asks 'जलबिन्दुनिपातेन क्रमशः कः पूर्यते?' — the घटः (pot) is gradually filled.

useCases.title: Patience lesson
useCases.description: A little study every day fills your 'pot' of knowledge over time.

useCases.title: Passive voice
useCases.description: पूर्यते = 'is filled' — a passive verb; the pot is the thing being filled.

useCases.title: Answer the exercise
useCases.description: कः पूर्यते? → घटः (the pot).

concepts.beyondTheBook: This verse continues: एवं विद्या च धर्मश्च — 'so too knowledge and dharma' accumulate drop by drop. It is the Sanskrit ancestor of 'little drops make the mighty ocean'.

questions.prompt: By how many 'व' (va) qualities does a person become honoured (पूजितः)?
solutionSteps: The verse lists विद्या, वपुस्, वाणी, वस्त्र, विनय — all starting with व.
The exercise answer to 'कतिभिः वकारैः?' is पञ्चभिः (five).
commonMistakes: Count the va-words in the verse — there are exactly five.

questions.prompt: How many faults (दोषाः) should a person desiring prosperity give up?
solutionSteps: The verse names six: निद्रा, तन्द्रा, भयम्, क्रोधः, आलस्यम्, दीर्घसूत्रता.
The exercise answer to 'कति दोषाः हातव्याः?' is षड् (six).
commonMistakes: List them out — sleep, drowsiness, fear, anger, laziness, procrastination = six.

questions.prompt: According to the verse, the intellect (बुद्धिः) is purified by —
solutionSteps: The verse: बुद्धिर्ज्ञानेन शुध्यति — the intellect is purified by knowledge.
Water cleans the body, truth the mind, knowledge the intellect.
commonMistakes: Water purifies the BODY (गात्राणि), not the intellect — match each means to its part.

solutionSteps: The verse: जलबिन्दुनिपातेन क्रमशः पूर्यते घटः — drop by drop the pot fills.
It teaches that small steady efforts accumulate.
commonMistakes: The image is a small घट (pot) filling drop by drop — not a lake or sea.

solutionSteps: सु ('good/well') + भाषित ('spoken') = 'well-said' — a wisdom verse.
The chapter calls them सुवचनानि, good sayings of the wise.
commonMistakes: सुभाषित is specifically a WISE saying, not just any speech.

topics.title: Words of Wisdom
topics.summary: Key vocabulary from the chapter's subhashitas.

concepts.title: प्रेरकः — One Who Inspires

explanations.kidFriendly: प्रेरकः means a person who inspires or motivates others. The chapter says everyone is capable (योग्यः), but a प्रेरकः — an inspiring guide — is rare and precious. Glossary: प्रेरणादायकः.
explanations.textbook: प्रेरकः — 'inspirer, motivator', glossed प्रेरणादायकः. From the verse 'अयोग्यः पुरुषो नास्ति योजकस्तत्र दुर्लभः' — no one is unworthy; a skilled organiser/motivator is what's rare.
explanations.expert: प्रेरकः is an agent-noun (-aka) from the causative of the root ईर् / प्र+ईर् ('to set in motion') — 'one who causes to move forward', i.e. a motivator.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's opening subhashita teaches that talent is everywhere; what is scarce (दुर्लभः) is the प्रेरकः who draws it out.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The full line — 'अयोग्यः पुरुषो नास्ति योजकस्तत्र दुर्लभः' — is a favourite leadership maxim: there are no useless people, only a shortage of those who can organise them well.

concepts.title: दीर्घसूत्रता — Procrastination

explanations.oneLine: दीर्घसूत्रता (dīrgha-sūtratā) — the habit of putting work off; procrastination.
explanations.kidFriendly: दीर्घसूत्रता is the habit of delaying — 'long-thread-ness', dragging a task out forever. It is one of the six faults the wise verse tells us to give up. Glossary: कार्य को आगे टालने की प्रवृत्ति.
explanations.textbook: दीर्घसूत्रता — 'procrastination', glossed विलम्बकार्यप्रवृत्तिः ('the tendency to delay work'). Listed among the षड् दोषाः to be abandoned.
explanations.expert: दीर्घ ('long') + सूत्र ('thread') + ता (abstract suffix) — literally 'long-threadedness', a vivid image of a task stretched out like an endless thread. The abstract suffix -ता turns the adjective into a noun ('the quality of').

concepts.reasoning: The chapter lists दीर्घसूत्रता as one of the six faults (षड् दोषाः) a person who wants to prosper must give up.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The -ता suffix (as in दीर्घसूत्रता) is the Sanskrit equivalent of English '-ness' — it builds an abstract noun from a quality, like सुन्दरता 'beauty' from सुन्दर 'beautiful'.

concepts.title: रिपुः — Enemy

explanations.kidFriendly: रिपुः means an enemy. In this chapter, laziness (आलस्यम्) is called a person's great enemy — a रिपुः you carry inside yourself. Glossary: शत्रुः.
explanations.textbook: रिपुः — 'enemy', glossed शत्रुः. The chapter's idea: आलस्यं ... महान् रिपुः — laziness is a person's greatest inner enemy.
explanations.expert: रिपुः is a masculine u-stem noun. Sanskrit has several words for 'enemy' (शत्रु, अरि, रिपु, वैरिन्); रिपु is common in verse for its rhythm.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's exercise 'आलस्यं केषां महान् रिपुः अस्ति?' frames laziness as the great enemy — using रिपुः for 'enemy'.

concepts.title: सङ्गतिः — Company / Association

explanations.kidFriendly: सङ्गतिः means the company you keep — who you associate with. Subhashitas repeatedly teach that good सङ्गतिः shapes a good person. Glossary: संसर्गः.
explanations.textbook: सङ्गतिः — 'company, association', glossed संसर्गः. A key theme of the chapter's moral verses: the company (सङ्गतिः) one keeps shapes one's character.
explanations.expert: सङ्गतिः is सम् ('together') + the root गम्/गत ('go') + ति (feminine action-noun) — 'a going-together', i.e. companionship. The -ति suffix forms feminine abstract/action nouns.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's wisdom verses stress that good सङ्गतिः (company) leads to good conduct — a recurring subhashita theme.

solutionSteps: The chapter glossary gives प्रेरकः = प्रेरणादायकः ('inspirer').
The opening verse says such a motivator (योजकः) is rare.
commonMistakes: प्रेरकः is the one who MOTIVATES others — not a lazy person.

solutionSteps: Glossary: दीर्घसूत्रता = the tendency to delay work (विलम्बकार्यप्रवृत्तिः).
Literally 'long-thread-ness' — stretching a task out endlessly.
commonMistakes: It is a FAULT (one of the six दोषाः) — the habit of delaying, not a virtue.

रिपुः = enemy (शत्रुः).
commonMistakes: Truth, knowledge and humility are virtues — the ENEMY here is laziness.

solutionSteps: Glossary: सङ्गतिः = संसर्गः ('association').
सम् + गति — 'a going-together', i.e. companionship.
commonMistakes: सङ्गतिः is about COMPANY/association, not food or festivals.

chapters.title: मित्राय नमः — Mitraya Namah (Salutation to the Sun)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 3. Students learn सूर्यनमस्कार (the Sun Salutation) from their teacher — a combination of postures, each paired with a mantra saluting the Sun by one of its twelve names (मित्राय नमः, रवये नमः …). The chapter teaches the dative case (चतुर्थी विभक्ति) that those mantras use, and the health, vigour, brilliance and wisdom the practice brings.

topics.title: सूर्यनमस्कारः — The Sun Salutation
topics.summary: The practice, its first mantra, the twelve names of the Sun, and its benefits.

concepts.title: सूर्यनमस्कारः — The Sun Salutation

explanations.oneLine: सूर्यनमस्कारः (sūrya-namaskāraḥ) — 'salutation to the Sun', a set of yoga postures.
explanations.kidFriendly: सूर्यनमस्कारः means 'salutation to the Sun'. The chapter explains it as a समाहारः (combination) of आसनानि (yoga postures) done facing the sun. Doing it daily gives a healthy body and mind.
explanations.textbook: सूर्यनमस्कारः — 'Sun-salutation', a समाहारः ('collection/combination') of आसनानि (postures). The chapter teaches that before each posture comes one मन्त्रः.
explanations.expert: सूर्यनमस्कारः is a tatpuruṣa compound: सूर्य ('sun') + नमस्कारः ('act of salutation', from नमस् 'bowing' + कार 'making'). Each posture is paired with a mantra addressed to the Sun.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's dialogue has students learning सूर्यनमस्कारः from their teacher (आचार्या) as a daily practice for health.

useCases.title: Do it daily
useCases.description: सूर्यनमस्कारः is a real morning exercise — the chapter recommends doing it प्रतिदिनम् (every day).

useCases.title: Break the word
useCases.description: सूर्य ('sun') + नमस्कारः ('salutation') = 'salutation to the Sun'.

useCases.title: Answer the exercise
useCases.description: An exercise asks how many postures (आसनानि) it combines.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Each of the twelve postures of सूर्यनमस्कार is traditionally paired with one of the Sun's twelve names — the practice unites movement, breath and mantra.

concepts.title: मित्राय नमः — The First Mantra (and the Dative Case)

explanations.oneLine: मित्राय नमः (mitrāya namaḥ) — 'salutation to Mitra (the Sun)'; नमः takes the dative case.
explanations.kidFriendly: मित्राय नमः means 'salutation to the Sun (Mitra)'. It is the FIRST mantra of सूर्यनमस्कार. Notice मित्राय — not मित्रः: when you say नमः ('salutation TO'), the word for whom you bow goes into the चतुर्थी विभक्ति (dative, the 'to/for' case).
explanations.textbook: मित्राय नमः — 'salutation to Mitra'. The chapter teaches that नमः governs the चतुर्थी विभक्ति (dative): मित्र → मित्राय ('to Mitra'). It is the first of the सूर्यनमस्कार mantras.
explanations.expert: नमः is one of the words that idiomatically takes the dative (चतुर्थी) of the one saluted — मित्राय ('to Mitra'). The chapter's शब्दरूप table shows the अकारान्त pattern: छात्र → छात्राय, नायक → नायकाय, आदित्य → आदित्याय.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter explicitly teaches the dative through these mantras: 'salutation TO X' puts X in the चतुर्थी विभक्ति, so मित्र becomes मित्राय.

useCases.title: Why मित्राय not मित्रः
useCases.description: नमः means 'salutation TO' — the 'to' is shown by the dative ending -आय.

useCases.title: First mantra
useCases.description: सूर्यनमस्कारस्य प्रथमः मन्त्रः = मित्राय नमः.

useCases.title: Pattern spotting
useCases.description: छात्र→छात्राय, आदित्य→आदित्याय: the अकारान्त dative adds -आय.

concepts.beyondTheBook: नमः, स्वाहा, स्वस्ति and अलम् are classic 'dative-governing' words in Sanskrit — wherever you greet, offer, or bless, the recipient takes the चतुर्थी.

concepts.title: सूर्यस्य द्वादश नामानि — The Twelve Names of the Sun

explanations.oneLine: The Sun has twelve names: मित्रः, रविः, सूर्यः, भानुः, खगः, पूषा, हिरण्यगर्भः, मरीचिः, आदित्यः, सविता, अर्कः, भास्करः.
explanations.kidFriendly: The Sun is called by many names. The chapter lists मित्रः, खगः, पूषा, रविः, भानुः, हिरण्यगर्भः, मरीचिः, सविता, अर्कः, भास्करः — all meaning 'the Sun'. In सूर्यनमस्कार, each of the twelve postures salutes the Sun by a different name.
explanations.textbook: The chapter's glossary groups मित्रः, खगः, पूषा, रविः, भानुः, हिरण्यगर्भः, मरीचिः, सविता, अर्कः, भास्करः (and आदित्यः) all under the meaning सूर्यः ('the Sun').
explanations.expert: Sanskrit prizes synonyms (एकार्थकशब्दाः); the Sun's twelve names each highlight a quality — सविता ('the impeller'), भास्करः ('the light-maker'), अर्कः ('the radiant'), पूषा ('the nourisher'). The सूर्यनमस्कार mantras cycle through them in the dative (मित्राय, रवये, …).

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches these as synonyms for the Sun, used across the twelve सूर्यनमस्कार mantras.

useCases.title: One Sun, many names
useCases.description: मित्रः, रविः, भास्करः all mean the Sun — Sanskrit loves rich synonyms.

useCases.title: Link to the practice
useCases.description: Each सूर्यनमस्कार posture salutes the Sun by a different name.

useCases.title: Meaning hints
useCases.description: भास्करः = 'light-maker', सविता = 'impeller', पूषा = 'nourisher'.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The names are not random: रवि gives us 'ravivāra' (Sunday), and भास्कर became the name of the great mathematician-astronomer Bhāskara — 'the one who makes light/knowledge'.

concepts.title: स्वस्थं शरीरम् — A Healthy Body and Mind

explanations.oneLine: स्वस्थम् (svastham) — 'healthy'; सूर्यनमस्कार gives a healthy body and mind.
explanations.kidFriendly: स्वस्थम् means 'healthy'. The chapter says that by doing सूर्यनमस्कार daily, people gain a स्वस्थं शरीरम् (healthy body) and a स्वस्थं मनः (healthy mind). Glossary: नीरोगम् ('free of disease').
explanations.textbook: स्वस्थम् — 'healthy', glossed नीरोगम्. The chapter states सूर्यनमस्कारेण ('by Sun-salutation') one attains a healthy body and mind.
explanations.expert: स्वस्थ literally means 'self-abiding' (स्व 'self' + स्थ 'standing') — 'settled in oneself', hence 'well, healthy'. A lovely Sanskrit insight: health is being centred in your own self.

concepts.reasoning: An exercise asks 'सूर्यनमस्कारेण जनाः कीदृशं शरीरं प्राप्नुवन्ति?' — people get a स्वस्थम् (healthy) body.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet स्वस्थम् in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 3; the glossary gives 'Healthy'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see स्वस्थम्, recall it means 'Healthy'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using स्वस्थम् ('Healthy').

concepts.beyondTheBook: The word स्वस्थ ('self-abiding = healthy') captures an idea modern wellness rediscovered: true health is being at ease within yourself, not just being disease-free.

questions.prompt: What is the first mantra of सूर्यनमस्कार?
solutionSteps: The chapter states सूर्यनमस्कारस्य प्रथमः मन्त्रः = मित्राय नमः.
मित्राय is the dative of मित्र ('the Sun/friend').
commonMistakes: All four are real Sun-salutation mantras, but the FIRST one is मित्राय नमः.

questions.prompt: In 'मित्राय नमः', why is it मित्राय and not मित्रः?
solutionSteps: नमः means 'salutation TO' — the one saluted goes into the चतुर्थी विभक्ति (dative).
मित्र → मित्राय, just like छात्र → छात्राय in the chapter's table.
commonMistakes: मित्राय is not plural — the -आय ending is the singular dative ('to Mitra').

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT used in the chapter as a name of the Sun?
solutionSteps: भास्करः, सविता, पूषा are all names of the Sun listed in the chapter.
रिपुः means 'enemy' (from Chapter 2) — not a Sun-name.
commonMistakes: रिपुः ('enemy') comes from Chapter 2; it is not one of the Sun's names.

questions.prompt: Doing सूर्यनमस्कार daily gives people a ___ body.
solutionSteps: The chapter says one attains a स्वस्थं शरीरम् ('healthy body') and स्वस्थं मनः ('healthy mind').
स्वस्थम् is glossed नीरोगम् ('disease-free').
commonMistakes: The whole point of the practice is HEALTH (स्वस्थम्), the opposite of sick or weak.

topics.title: चतुर्थी विभक्तिः + Words
topics.summary: The dative ('to/for') case taught by the mantras, plus key vocabulary.

concepts.title: चतुर्थी विभक्तिः — The Dative ('to / for') Case

explanations.oneLine: चतुर्थी विभक्तिः — the dative case, the 'to/for' form; अकारान्त nouns add -आय (छात्र → छात्राय).
explanations.kidFriendly: The चतुर्थी विभक्ति (dative, the fourth case) is the 'to/for' form. The chapter's table shows masculine अकारान्त nouns: छात्र → छात्राय ('to a student'), नायक → नायकाय, आदित्य → आदित्याय. Feminine आकारान्त: आचार्या → आचार्यायै.
explanations.textbook: चतुर्थी विभक्तिः (dative). अकारान्त-पुंलिङ्गम् singular: stem + -आय (छात्राय, नायकाय, आदित्याय). आकारान्त-स्त्रीलिङ्गम् singular: -आयै (आचार्यायै, योगितायै). Used after नमः.
explanations.expert: The dative marks the indirect object / recipient ('to/for whom'). The chapter teaches it through नमः-mantras: salute TO the Sun → मित्राय (dative). The dual/plural forms (-आभ्याम्, -एभ्यः) appear in the same table.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches the dative specifically so students understand why salutation-mantras say मित्राय, रवये, सवित्रे — the Sun is the one saluted 'to'.

useCases.title: Spot the 'to/for'
useCases.description: When English would say 'to X' or 'for X', Sanskrit often uses the चतुर्थी.

useCases.title: Memorise the ending
useCases.description: अकारान्त masculine dative singular = stem + -आय (छात्राय).

useCases.title: Use with नमः
useCases.description: नमः + dative = 'salutation to ___' (मित्राय नमः).

concepts.beyondTheBook: Sanskrit has eight cases (अष्ट विभक्तयः); the dative (चतुर्थी) is the fourth. Learning one full paradigm (like छात्र) unlocks hundreds of similar अकारान्त nouns.

concepts.title: प्रज्ञा — Wisdom / Intelligence

explanations.kidFriendly: प्रज्ञा means wisdom or sharp intelligence. The chapter mentions that practices like सूर्यनमस्कार help develop प्रज्ञा. Glossary: मेधा ('intellect').
explanations.textbook: प्रज्ञा — 'wisdom/intelligence', glossed मेधा. A feminine noun for the highest, discerning kind of intelligence.
explanations.expert: प्रज्ञा is प्र ('forth, deeply') + the root ज्ञा ('to know') — 'deep/forward knowing', i.e. insight. It is the same प्रज्ञा as in the Buddhist 'prajñā' (transcendent wisdom).

concepts.reasoning: The chapter associates physical and spiritual practice with the growth of प्रज्ञा (wisdom) and तेजः (brilliance).

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet प्रज्ञा in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 3; the glossary gives 'Intelligence / Wisdom'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see प्रज्ञा, recall it means 'Intelligence / Wisdom'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using प्रज्ञा ('Intelligence / Wisdom').

concepts.beyondTheBook: प्रज्ञा (deep knowing, from प्र+ज्ञा) is a step beyond ordinary बुद्धि — it is the discerning wisdom that the whole tradition of learning aims at.

concepts.title: तेजः — Brilliance / Radiance

explanations.kidFriendly: तेजः means brilliance or radiant energy — like the shining glow of the Sun. The chapter uses it for the inner radiance one gains. Glossary: दीप्तिः ('shine').
explanations.textbook: तेजः — 'brilliance, splendour', glossed दीप्तिः. A neuter s-stem noun; fittingly used in a chapter about the radiant Sun.
explanations.expert: तेजस् is a neuter -as stem (तेजः in nominative/accusative) from the root तिज् ('to be sharp/bright'). It means both physical brilliance and the inner 'fire'/vitality of a person.

concepts.reasoning: In this Sun-themed chapter, तेजः ('radiance') is both the Sun's light and the inner brilliance the practice is said to give.

concepts.title: वीर्यम् — Vigour / Valour

explanations.kidFriendly: वीर्यम् means vigour or manly strength/valour. The chapter links daily practice to gaining वीर्यम्. Glossary: पराक्रमः ('prowess').
explanations.textbook: वीर्यम् — 'vigour/valour', glossed पराक्रमः. A neuter noun; one of the qualities strengthened by सूर्यनमस्कार in the chapter.
explanations.expert: वीर्यम् derives from वीर ('hero') + -य (abstract suffix) — 'the quality of a hero', i.e. vigour, valour, energy.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter presents वीर्यम् (vigour) alongside तेजः and प्रज्ञा as benefits of disciplined daily practice.

questions.prompt: The 'चतुर्थी विभक्ति' (fourth case) is used to express —
solutionSteps: The dative (चतुर्थी) marks the one TO/FOR whom — e.g. छात्राय 'to a student'.
नमः + dative = 'salutation TO ___'.
commonMistakes: 'Of' is the genitive (षष्ठी); 'from' is the ablative — the चतुर्थी is specifically 'to/for'.

questions.prompt: The dative singular of the masculine अकारान्त noun 'छात्र' is —
solutionSteps: The chapter's table gives छात्र → छात्राय (dative singular).
अकारान्त masculine dative singular adds -आय.
commonMistakes: छात्रः is nominative, छात्रम् accusative, छात्रस्य genitive — the dative is छात्राय.

solutionSteps: Glossary: प्रज्ञा = मेधा ('intellect/wisdom').
प्र + ज्ञा = 'deep knowing' — insight.
commonMistakes: प्रज्ञा is deep wisdom, not a feeling like tiredness or anger.

solutionSteps: Glossary: तेजः = दीप्तिः ('shine, brilliance').
Fitting for a chapter about the radiant Sun.
commonMistakes: तेजः is RADIANCE/brilliance — the opposite of darkness.

chapters.title: न लभ्यते चेत् आम्लं द्राक्षाफलम् — The Fox and the Grapes
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 4 — the Sanskrit retelling of 'The Fox and the Grapes'. A tired, thirsty fox finds a grape-vine, jumps for the grapes again and again, and — unable to reach them — declares they must be sour anyway. The chapter teaches the moral of not belittling what we fail to get, plus the -तः direction words (left/right/front/behind) and vocabulary of thirst, hunger and tiredness.

topics.title: शृगालः द्राक्षा च — The Fox and the Grapes
topics.summary: The fable, its characters, and its 'sour grapes' moral.

concepts.title: शृगालः — The Fox

explanations.oneLine: शृगालः (śṛgālaḥ) — 'a fox / jackal', the main character of the story.
explanations.kidFriendly: शृगालः means a fox (or jackal). He is the hero of this story — a thirsty, hungry fox who finds a grape-vine. Glossary: लोमशा ('the furry one').
explanations.textbook: शृगालः — 'fox/jackal', glossed लोमशा. The protagonist of the chapter's fable, wandering the वनम् (forest), श्रान्तः (tired) and पिपासायुक्तः (thirsty).
explanations.expert: शृगालः is a masculine अकारान्त noun. In Sanskrit fable tradition (Pañcatantra, Hitopadeśa) the शृगाल is a stock clever-but-vain character — exactly his role here.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's story opens with a शृगालः roaming the forest, tired and thirsty, who then spots a grape-vine.

concepts.title: द्राक्षालता — The Grape-Vine

explanations.kidFriendly: द्राक्षालता means a grape-vine — the climbing plant with bunches of grapes. The fox sees the grapes hanging उपरि (above) him. Glossary: द्राक्षाफलस्य वल्लीम् ('the creeper of grape-fruit').
explanations.textbook: द्राक्षालताम् — accusative of द्राक्षालता, 'grape-vine', glossed द्राक्षाफलस्य वल्लीम्. The grapes hang उपरि (above), out of the fox's reach.
explanations.expert: द्राक्षालता is a compound: द्राक्षा ('grape') + लता ('creeper/vine'). The grapes being उपरि ('above') sets up the whole problem — they are out of reach.

concepts.reasoning: In the story the fox finds a द्राक्षालता with ripe grapes hanging above him, which he cannot reach.

concepts.title: उत्पतति — He Jumps Up

explanations.kidFriendly: उत्पतति means 'jumps up'. The fox jumps up पुनः पुनः (again and again) trying to reach the grapes — once (एकवारम्), twice (द्विवारम्), many times. Glossary: कूर्दते ('leaps').
explanations.textbook: उत्पतति — 'leaps up', glossed कूर्दते. The fox उत्पतति एकवारम् द्विवारम् पुनः पुनः ('jumps once, twice, again and again') but cannot reach the grapes.
explanations.expert: उत्पतति = उत् ('up') + पतति ('falls/flies', from पत्). The prefix उत् flips पत् ('fall') into 'fly/leap upward' — a neat example of how Sanskrit prefixes (उपसर्ग) change a verb's direction.

concepts.reasoning: The story's tension comes from उत्पतति: the fox keeps jumping up, again and again, but the grapes stay out of reach.

concepts.beyondTheBook: उत् + पत् → उत्पतति ('leap up'); the same पत् with नि gives निपतति ('fall down'), with आ gives आपतति ('rush toward'). One root, many directions via prefixes.

concepts.title: आम्लम् — 'Sour!' (the fable's moral)

explanations.oneLine: आम्लम् (āmlam) — 'sour'; the fox declares the grapes sour because he can't reach them.
explanations.kidFriendly: आम्लम् means 'sour'. When the fox cannot reach the grapes, he gives up and says they must be आम्लम् (sour) anyway — so he didn't want them! The title न लभ्यते चेत् आम्लं द्राक्षाफलम् means 'if it isn't obtained, the grape is (called) sour'. The lesson: don't belittle what you fail to get.
explanations.textbook: आम्लम् — 'sour', glossed आम्लरसयुक्तम्. The fox, unable to reach the द्राक्षाफलम्, declares it आम्लम् — the origin of the saying 'sour grapes'.
explanations.expert: The title is a conditional: न लभ्यते चेत् ('if it is not obtained') आम्लं द्राक्षाफलम् ('the grape-fruit [is called] sour'). चेत् marks the condition. The fable names a universal human habit — devaluing what we cannot have.

concepts.reasoning: The whole story builds to the fox calling the unreachable grapes आम्लम् (sour) — teaching us not to despise what we fail to achieve.

questions.prompt: Who is the main character of this chapter's story?
solutionSteps: The story is about a शृगालः (fox/jackal), glossed लोमशा.
He is tired and thirsty and finds a grape-vine.
commonMistakes: The other animals don't appear — the hero is the शृगालः (fox).

solutionSteps: Glossary: उत्पतति = कूर्दते ('leaps').
उत् ('up') + पतति → 'leaps up'. The fox jumps up again and again.
commonMistakes: उत्पतति is JUMPING UP (to reach the grapes), not sleeping or eating.

questions.prompt: When the fox cannot reach the grapes, what does he say they are?
solutionSteps: Unable to reach them, the fox declares the grapes आम्लम् (sour).
The title: न लभ्यते चेत् आम्लं द्राक्षाफलम् — 'if not obtained, the grape is sour'.
commonMistakes: He calls them SOUR (आम्लम्) as an excuse — the famous 'sour grapes'.

questions.prompt: What is the lesson (moral) of this fable?
options: don't belittle what you fail to get
questions.answer: don't belittle what you fail to get
solutionSteps: The fox calls the grapes 'sour' only because he couldn't reach them.
Moral: we should not despise or devalue what we fail to achieve.
commonMistakes: The story is specifically about making excuses for failure ('sour grapes'), not about sharing or waking early.

topics.title: दिशाशब्दाः — Direction Words (-तः) + Vocabulary
topics.summary: The तसिल् direction adverbs and key story vocabulary.

concepts.title: तसिल् दिशाशब्दाः — Direction Words (-तः)

explanations.oneLine: वामतः, दक्षिणतः, अग्रतः, पृष्ठतः — 'on the left, on the right, in front, behind' (the -तः suffix).
explanations.kidFriendly: Sanskrit makes direction words by adding -तः to a base: वामतः (on the left), दक्षिणतः (on the right), अग्रतः (in front), पृष्ठतः (behind). The chapter teaches this set together.
explanations.textbook: The chapter's glossary lists वामतः (वामभागे, 'on the left'), दक्षिणतः (दक्षिणभागे, 'on the right'), अग्रतः (अग्रभागे, 'in front'), पृष्ठतः (पृष्ठभागे, 'behind') — all formed with the तसिल् suffix -तः.
explanations.expert: These are तसिल्-pratyaya adverbs: a base + तः meaning 'from/at/towards that side'. वाम→वामतः, दक्षिण→दक्षिणतः, अग्र→अग्रतः, पृष्ठ→पृष्ठतः. The -तः ending is indeclinable (अव्यय).

concepts.reasoning: The chapter groups these four direction-adverbs so students learn the -तः pattern as one family.

concepts.title: पिपासा / तृषा — Thirst

explanations.kidFriendly: पिपासा (also तृषा) means thirst. The fox is wandering श्रान्तः (tired) and full of पिपासा (thirst) when he finds the grapes. Glossary: पातुम् इच्छा ('the wish to drink').
explanations.textbook: पिपासा — 'thirst', glossed पातुम् इच्छा. तृषा is its synonym (glossed पिपासा). Both describe the fox's condition at the story's start.
explanations.expert: पिपासा is a desiderative noun from पा ('to drink') — 'the wish to drink', exactly parallel to जिज्ञासा ('wish to know', from ज्ञा) in Chapter 1. Recognising this पा→पिपासा pattern links the chapters.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter describes the fox as thirsty (पिपासा/तृषा) — the reason he wants the grapes' juice.

concepts.title: श्रान्तः — Tired

explanations.kidFriendly: श्रान्तः means tired. The fox is श्रान्तः (tired) and खिन्नः (sad) from wandering before he finds the grape-vine. Glossary: क्लान्तः ('weary').
explanations.textbook: श्रान्तः — 'tired', glossed क्लान्तः. Describes the fox's state, paired with खिन्नः ('sad').
explanations.expert: श्रान्तः is the past-participle of श्रम् ('to be weary, to toil') — literally 'one who has toiled/grown weary'. Past participles in -त are everywhere in Sanskrit narrative ('having done X').

concepts.reasoning: The chapter sets the scene with a श्रान्तः (tired) and खिन्नः (sad) fox, making his hope for the grapes vivid.

concepts.beyondTheBook: श्रान्त comes from श्रम् ('toil') — the same root as परिश्रम ('hard work') and श्रमिक ('worker'). Being श्रान्त is the result of श्रम.

solutionSteps: वाम = left; वामतः = 'on the left side' (वामभागे).
The -तः suffix makes direction adverbs.
commonMistakes: दक्षिणतः = right, अग्रतः = front, पृष्ठतः = behind — only वामतः is 'left'.

questions.prompt: The direction words वामतः, दक्षिणतः, अग्रतः, पृष्ठतः are all formed by adding which suffix?
solutionSteps: All four end in -तः (the तसिल् suffix), meaning 'in/at that direction'.
वाम→वामतः, अग्र→अग्रतः.
commonMistakes: -आय is dative, -स्य genitive, -ेन instrumental — the direction suffix here is -तः.

solutionSteps: Glossary: पिपासा = पातुम् इच्छा ('the wish to drink') = thirst.
तृषा is its synonym.
commonMistakes: Hunger is बुभुक्षा; पिपासा is specifically THIRST (the wish to drink).

solutionSteps: Glossary: श्रान्तः = क्लान्तः ('weary/tired').
From the root श्रम् ('to toil').
commonMistakes: श्रान्तः means TIRED (from toiling) — not happy or angry.
